description:
The observer look-angle pipeline (RA/Dec/alt-az for celestial bodies and satellites) uses a spherical Earth model throughout, but the input latitude comes from WGS84-sourced coordinates (Geolocation API, timezone table) with no geodetic-to-geocentric conversion. The `equatorialToHorizontal` and `observerEci` functions treat the latitude as geocentric directly in spherical trigonometry, producing position and angle errors: up to ~0.2° in altitude for celestial bodies (from latitude mismatch) and ~1–3° in satellite look-angles (from the combined latitude + radius error at ~400 km range, dominated by the observer's surface position being wrong by up to 21 km at the poles). The code explicitly acknowledges this at `src/lib/satellite/look-angles.ts` line 10: `const RE = 6378.137; // km (spherical Earth; ellipsoid/altitude refinement later)`.

Expected: Input WGS84 geodetic latitude should be correctly transformed into the internal model — either by converting to geocentric latitude before use in spherical formulas, or by implementing the full WGS84 ellipsoid observer position (prime vertical radius, ellipsoid height h=0 for the nominal case). For celestial bodies, the topocentric parallax should use the latitude-dependent Earth radius instead of the constant equatorial radius. All three invariants should hold when WGS84 geodetic coordinates are the input.

Acceptance criteria:
- The direction of the J2000 vernal equinox (ecliptic +x, vector (1,0,0)) when passed through eclipticToEquatorial must yield RA = 0 rad and Dec = 0 rad — unchanged after applying the ecliptic-to-equatorial x-axis rotation by the mean obliquity [code-invariant: definition of the J2000 coordinate system: the equinox direction is shared by both ecliptic and equatorial frames, so RA=0/Dec=0 at that point]
- The ecliptic north pole direction (ecliptic +z, vector (0,0,1)) when passed through eclipticToEquatorial must yield Dec = 90° − mean_obliquity(jd) — approximately 66.56° at J2000 [code-invariant: geometric relationship: the equatorial north pole is separated from the ecliptic north pole by the obliquity ε, so the ecliptic north pole projects to Dec = 90° − ε in equatorial coordinates]
- A body whose declination equals the observer's WGS84 geodetic latitude, placed on the local meridian (local hour angle H = 0), must yield altitude = 90° (zenith) when passed through the full pipeline (skyPosition or equatorialToHorizontal), after correcting geodetic latitude to geocentric latitude [reporter: invariant of the equatorial-to-horizontal transformation on the WGS84 ellipsoid — the observer's zenith direction projects onto the celestial sphere at declination equal to the observer's geodetic latitude when the body is on the meridian]

Domain facts:
- WGS84 ellipsoid: a = 6378.137 km (semi-major axis), b = 6356.752314245 km (semi-minor axis), f = 1/298.257223563 (flattening), e² = 2f − f² ≈ 0.00669438
- Geocentric latitude φ' relates to geodetic latitude φ via: tan(φ') = (1 − f)² · tan(φ), or equivalently: z/(N(1−e²)) = sin(φ′), where N = a/√(1−e²·sin²φ) is the prime vertical radius of curvature
- The topocentric parallax in altitude is: π ≈ asin(R_obs / Δ), where R_obs is the observer's geocentric distance (not the equatorial radius), and Δ is the body's geocentric distance
- The difference between geodetic and geocentric latitude reaches a maximum of ~0.19° at ±45° latitude
